abstract: Macrophages are innate immune cells that primarily function as professional phagocytes, playing essential roles throughout the body in host defense and maintaining homeostasis. The CNS is populated by two anatomically distinct macrophage populations; parenchymal microglia and border-resident CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs). These populations coordinate the neuroinflammatory response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and are exposed to distinct microenvironmental cues that could shape their functions. CNS macrophages are also involved in infection with neurotropic viruses such as HIV, where the persistent infection contributes to chronic neuroinflammation and the constellation of other neurological symptoms collectively termed neuroHIV. Although antiretroviral therapy (cART) has transformed HIV care and lessened the severity of many neuroHIV symptoms, the persistence of CNS viral reservoirs and neurological deficits remains a major comorbidity and barrier to cure. Understanding specific contributions of microglia and CAMs to inflammation and neuroHIV has been challenging due to the lack of genetically matched human model systems enabling direct mechanistic comparison between of microglia and CAMs. To address this, we optimized the generation of syngeneic, human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived microglia-like (iMg) and CAM-like (iMacs) cells. These are generated simultaneously from a single donor line and have the same genetic background, enabling side-by-side characterization and functional analyses of inflammation and HIV infection. Transcriptomic profiling by RNA sequencing revealed substantial baseline differences in inflammatory and immune signaling pathways between iMg and iMacs. These intrinsic differences were also observed in TLR-specific NF-{kappa}B responses. Stimulation of TLR4 drove heightened response in iMg relative to iMac, correlating closely with morphological changes, while stimulating TLR2 had a contrasting effect, eliciting a stronger and more robust early NF-{kappa}B response in iMacs. In HIV infection studies, iMacs were more permissive to viral replication at baseline, whereas iMg showed a reduced susceptibility to infection. However, iMacs responded more robustly to cART, while iMg exhibited relative resistance to cART-mediated suppression. These findings delineate fundamental inflammatory and virologic differences between human microglia and CAMs and provide a robust foundation on which to further examine HIV infection, cART efficacy, and immune function in these distinct CNS myeloid populations.
